newsitem.title: USA: Cyrix up on Compaq deal, Intel off.
newsitem.headline: Cyrix up on Compaq deal, Intel off.

text.p: Shares of Cyrix Corp jumped after the company said it will supply Compaq Computer Corp with a new low-cost microprocessor for personal computers selling for less than $1,000, analysts said.

Cyrix jumped 3-7/8 to close at $29-3/8, and Intel Corp, which dominates the PC microprocessor market, slid 4 to 149-7/8. Intel was the most heavily traded Nasdaq issue with volume of more than 15 million shares, with Cyrix fourth in Nasdaq volume.
Analysts said the Cyrix MediaGX chip, which includes video graphics and sound functions on one chip, may open a promising new market, but would not threaten Intel's commanding lead.
"A few competitive wins does not loosen the giant's grip," said David Wu, high tech analyst at ABN AMRO Chicago Corp.

Compaq said its Presario 2000 series, equipped with the Cyrix chip, will be priced at $1,000 plus around $300 for a monitor and be aimed at families looking to buy a second computer or first-time buyers seeking an affordable machine.
Compaq shares fell 1/2 to 87-7/8 as tech shares weakened.

Analysts said they did not expect Intel to concede even the low end of the market to the much smaller Cyrix, however, and noted that Compaq and Intel have worked closely despite past tensions over sourcing processors from Intel's rivals.
That sentiment was echoed by Intel.

"Our relationship with Compaq is very, very strong and very healthy right now," said Intel spokesman Howard High, adding that Intel supplies lower-end processors, such as 120- and 130-megahertz Pentiums at volume prices of around $100 for use in PCs which are already selling for under $1,000.
These chips would have a performance above the projected performance of the new Cyrix chip, although the entry-level Intel chips would not include the video and sound functions.
"At the end of the day this is a marketplace that's very competitive," High said. "We try to keep our product lines fresh and try to keep ouur prices aggressive."

Cowen & Co semiconductor analyst Drew Peck said he estimates the new MediaGX chips will account for roughly half of the estimated 3.5 million Cyrix microprocessors expected to ship in 1997, although a much smaller portion of the company's revenues due to the lower price points.
A key issue would be how quickly the Richardson, Texas-based company, which contracts out its production, will be able to drive down costs of making the chips.
"It's actually a very fine architecture they've come up with," said Peck, adding of the pricing "in many respects it's almost too aggressive."

Peck said it would be "a significant challenge" to build and sell the chip for $99 and still make money. He therefore was not expecting a significant profits contribution from the chip in the near-term for Cyrix.
"It's an extremely attractive price point," however, he added. "The question is how much are customers willing to compromise on the state of the art performance versus cost."
This was critical not only for Cyrix, but also for PC makers aiming to increase the share of U.S. homes owning personal computers to above the current 35 percent level.

Cyrix is not the only semiconductor company still aiming to chip away at Intel's huge microprocessor business. Advanced Micro Devices, whose shares rose 3/8 to 36-3/8 today, is also pitching its new K6 design for high-end notebooks.

Wu said AMD could make inroads, but he still expects all rivals combined to make less than 10 percent of the $21.4 billion in 1997 microprocessor sales he projects for Intel. Wu estimates Intel currently has close to 95 percent of the market for higher-end, Intel Pentium and above performance microprocessors based on the PC architecture, and he does not see this shifting dramatically any time soon. (( --sam.perry@reuters.com, Palo Alto Bureau +1 415 846 5400))
